source_refs.note: Book p. 72: 3.1.1 Rule-1 (constant), Rule-2 (sum and difference), Rule-3 (power rule), the General Power Rule, Rule-4 (f'/f) and Rule-5 (linear substitution).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Every rule below is a differentiation rule read backwards. So each one can be checked in one line: differentiate the right-hand side and you get the integrand back. Learn the rule together with that check; then you never need to memorise blindly.
Rule-1: \(\int k\,f(x)\,dx = k\int f(x)\,dx\) (Integration of function with constant (k)).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why: \(\frac{d}{dx}\big(k\,F(x)\big) = k\,F'(x)\). A constant factor stays outside during differentiation, so it stays outside during integration too.
When: the integrand has a number (or a constant letter) multiplied in front.
Our example: \(\int 5x^{2}\,dx = 5\int x^{2}\,dx = 5 \cdot \frac{x^{3}}{3} + c = \frac{5}{3}x^{3} + c\).
Only a constant may be taken out. \(\int x \cdot x\,dx\) is not \(x\int x\,dx\), because \(x\) is not a constant.
Rule-2: \(\int [f(x) \pm g(x)]\,dx = \int f(x)\,dx \pm \int g(x)\,dx\) (Sum and Difference Rule).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why: the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, so an integral of a sum may be split term by term.
When: the integrand is several terms joined by \(+\) or \(-\). Integrate each term separately and write one \(+\,c\) at the end (the constants of all terms combine into one).
Our example: \(\int (6x^{2} - \cos x)\,dx = 2x^{3} - \sin x + c\).
There is no such rule for a product: \(\int x \cdot x\,dx = \frac{x^{3}}{3} + c\), but \(\int x\,dx \cdot \int x\,dx\) would give \(\frac{x^{4}}{4}\). A product must first be multiplied out (or handled by later methods).
Rule-3: \(\int x^{n}\,dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + c\), where \(n \ne -1\) (The Power Rule).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why: differentiate the answer:
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\right) = \dfrac{(n+1)x^{n}}{n+1}\]
\[= x^{n}\]
In words: add 1 to the power, then divide by the new power. It is exactly the reverse of the derivative rule 'multiply by the power, then subtract 1'.
Why \(n \ne -1\)? For \(n = -1\) the new power is 0 and we would divide by 0. That case, \(\int \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \ln|x| + c\), is in the table of 3.1.2.
The rule works for every real \(n \ne -1\): negative and fractional powers too. First write roots and reciprocals as powers.
Our examples: \(\int x^{4}\,dx = \frac{x^{5}}{5} + c\); \(\int x^{-3}\,dx = \frac{x^{-2}}{-2} + c = -\frac{1}{2x^{2}} + c\); \(\int \sqrt{x}\,dx = \int x^{1/2}\,dx = \frac{x^{3/2}}{3/2} + c = \frac{2}{3}x^{3/2} + c\).
The General Power Rule: \(\int [f(x)]^{n} f'(x)\,dx = \frac{[f(x)]^{n+1}}{n+1} + c\), where \(n \ne -1\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why: by the chain rule,
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{[f(x)]^{n+1}}{n+1}\right) = [f(x)]^{n} f'(x)\]
When: you see a bracket raised to a power, multiplied by the derivative of what is inside the bracket. Treat the whole bracket like \(x\) in the power rule.
Our examples: \(\int (x^{2} + 1)^{3}\,2x\,dx = \frac{(x^{2} + 1)^{4}}{4} + c\), because \(2x\) is the derivative of \(x^{2} + 1\). Similarly \(\int (x^{3} + 5)^{2}\,3x^{2}\,dx = \frac{(x^{3} + 5)^{3}}{3} + c\).
If the derivative of the bracket is missing, the rule cannot be used: \(\int (x^{2} + 1)^{3}\,dx\) is not \(\frac{(x^{2} + 1)^{4}}{4} + c\) (expand it instead).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why: by the chain rule \(\frac{d}{dx}\ln|f(x)| = \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\).
When: the integrand is a fraction whose numerator is the derivative of its denominator. This is the \(n = -1\) case of the General Power Rule, which the power rule cannot handle.
Our example: \(\int \frac{2x}{x^{2} + 5}\,dx = \ln|x^{2} + 5| + c = \ln(x^{2} + 5) + c\), since \(x^{2} + 5 > 0\).
If the numerator is the derivative only up to a constant factor, fix the constant with Rule-1: \(\int \frac{x}{x^{2} + 5}\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\int \frac{2x}{x^{2} + 5}\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\ln(x^{2} + 5) + c\).
The absolute value is needed because \(\ln\) is defined only for positive numbers, while \(f(x)\) may be negative.

Rule-5: If \(f'\) is the derivative of \(f\), and \(\int f'(x)\,dx = f(x) + c\), then for any constants \(a \ne 0\) and \(b\), \(\int f'(ax+b)\,dx = \frac{f(ax+b)}{a} + c\). (Linear Substitution Rule).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why: by the chain rule \(\frac{d}{dx}f(ax+b) = a\,f'(ax+b)\). The derivative brings out an extra factor \(a\), so the integral must divide by \(a\).
When: a function you already know how to integrate, with \(x\) replaced by a linear expression \(ax + b\).
Our examples: \(\int \cos(3x + 2)\,dx = \frac{\sin(3x + 2)}{3} + c\); \(\int (2x + 1)^{5}\,dx = \frac{(2x + 1)^{6}}{6 \cdot 2} + c = \frac{(2x + 1)^{6}}{12} + c\); \(\int e^{4x - 1}\,dx = \frac{e^{4x - 1}}{4} + c\).
It works only for a linear inside \(ax + b\). For \(\int \cos(x^{2})\,dx\) dividing by the derivative of \(x^{2}\) is wrong.

a bracket to a power times the derivative of the bracket

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Rule-1: constants come out of the integral. Rule-2: integrate term by term.
2. Rule-3 (power rule): \(\int x^{n}\,dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + c\), \(n \ne -1\); add 1 to the power, divide by the new power.
3. General Power Rule: a bracket to a power times the bracket's derivative.
4. Rule-4: numerator = derivative of denominator gives \(\ln|\text{denominator}| + c\).
5. Rule-5: for \(ax + b\) inside, integrate as usual and divide by \(a\).
6. Check every answer by differentiating it.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Splitting a product: \(\int f(x)g(x)\,dx \ne \int f(x)\,dx \cdot \int g(x)\,dx\).
2. Using the power rule for \(n = -1\): \(\int x^{-1}\,dx\) is \(\ln|x| + c\), never \(\frac{x^{0}}{0}\).
3. Forgetting to divide by \(a\) in Rule-5: \(\int (2x+1)^{5}\,dx \ne \frac{(2x+1)^{6}}{6} + c\).
4. Using Rule-4 when the top is not the derivative of the bottom: \(\int \frac{1}{x^{2} + 1}\,dx \ne \ln(x^{2} + 1) + c\) (it is \(\tan^{-1}x + c\), see 3.1.2).
5. Using the General Power Rule without \(f'(x)\) present: \(\int (x^{2} + 1)^{3}\,dx \ne \frac{(x^{2} + 1)^{4}}{4} + c\).
